1                              III.  REMAND                                  
2       Plaintiffs have moved to remand the case for lack of jurisdiction. Defendants contend that 
3  the SAC is removable under the Class Action Fairness Act of 2005, 28 U.S.C. §§ 1332(d), 1453, 
4  1711–1715 (“CAFA”).5 Dkt. # 1 ¶ 9. Plaintiffs argue that federal jurisdiction under CAFA does 
5  not lie for two reasons: (1) the CAFA numerosity requirement, 28 U.S.C. § 1332(d)(5)(B), has 
6  not been met; and (2) the “securities exception” to CAFA, 28 U.S.C. §§ 1332(d)(9), 1453(d) 
7  applies. Defendants contest both arguments.                               
8  A.   Legal Standard for Removal and Burden of Proof                       
9       CAFA amended § 1332 and added § 1453 to title 28 of the United States Code, and these 
10  sections govern federal jurisdiction under CAFA. In particular, there are two key CAFA 
11  provisions underlying the parties’ dispute in this matter. First, under CAFA, federal jurisdiction 
12  exists only where the numerosity requirement is met, i.e., “where the aggregate number of 
13  members of a proposed plaintiff class is 100 or more.” Benko v. Quality Loan Serv. Corp., 789 
14  F.3d 1111, 1116 (9th Cir. 2015); 28 U.S.C. § 1332(d)(5)(B). Second, Congress excluded certain 
15  types of claims from federal jurisdiction under CAFA, including claims regarding “rights, duties 
16  (including fiduciary duties), and obligations relating to or created by or pursuant to any 
17  security.” 28 U.S.C. § 1332(d)(9)(C); 28 U.S.C. § 1453(d)(3). This exclusion is colloquially 
18  known as the “securities exception.” See, e.g., Eminence Inv’rs, L.L.L.P. v. Bank of New York 
19  Mellon, 782 F.3d 504, 505–10 (9th Cir. 2015).                            
20      “The party seeking a federal forum has the burden of establishing that federal jurisdiction 
21  is proper.” Xavier v. Allstate Prop. & Cas. Ins. Co., C12-00920 RAJ, 2012 WL 13024685, at *1 
22  (W.D. Wash. Aug. 29, 2012) (citing Abrego Abrego v. Dow Chem. Corp., 443 F.3d 676, 682–
23  83 (9th Cir. 2006)). The parties appear to agree on who bears the burden of proving the 
24  numerosity requirement. See Dkts. # 7 at 5–6, # 17 at 4–5 (discussing the burden of proof). 
25  Where a state court defendant removes a putative class action from state court, the defendant

19      has the burden to show that one of these provisions applies. Id.

3  B.   CAFA Numerosity Requirement                                          
4       As stated above, federal jurisdiction exists under CAFA only “where the aggregate 
5  number of members of a proposed plaintiff class is 100 or more.” Benko, 789 F.3d at 1116; 28 
6  U.S.C. § 1332(d)(5)(B). The proposed class at issue here is defined as “[a]ll [VoiceBox 
7  shareholders] who did not have the opportunity to approve or disapprove the Nuance 
8  Transaction and did not release claims relating to the Nuance Transaction.” SAC ¶ 4.38. When 
9  evaluating a CAFA jurisdictional requirement, a district court may consider whether the 
10  requirement is “facially apparent” from the complaint, and if not, the court may consider 
11  “summary-judgment-type evidence.” Abrego Abrego, 443 F.3d at 690 (quoting Singer v. State 
12  Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. Co., 116 F.3d 373, 377 (9th Cir. 1997) (analyizing the amount in 
13  controversy requirement)). The Supreme Court has generally characterized a party’s burden of 
14  proving federal jurisdiction in terms of “preponderance of evidence.” See McNutt v. Gen. 
15  Motors Acceptance Corp. of Ind., 298 U.S. 178, 189 (1936) (discussing a party’s burden to 
16  show that federal jurisdiction is appropriate and that he “justify his allegations by a 
17  preponderance of evidence”). And “[d]istrict courts have applied the preponderance of the 
18  evidence standard to CAFA’s 100-person numerosity requirement.” Fergerstrom v. PNC Bank, 
19  N.A., No. CIV. 13-00526 DKW, 2014 WL 1669101, at *9 (D. Haw. Apr. 25, 2014) (citing 
20  Kitazato v. Black Diamond Hospitality Invs., LLC, Civ. No. 09–00271 DAE–LEK, 2009 WL 
21  3824851, at *1 (D. Haw. Nov. 13, 2009); Coit v. Fidelity Assurance Assocs., LLC, No. 08–
22  0285, 2008 WL 3286978, at *4 (N.D. Cal. Aug. 6, 2008)).

15  regarding “rights, duties (including fiduciary duties), and obligations relating to or created by or

20      Defendants also argue that it would be more consistent with the overall purpose and 
21  objectives of CAFA to construe the security exception as inapplicable to the present action. The 
22  Supreme Court has explained that CAFA’s “provisions should be read broadly, with a strong

574 U.S. 81

25  (discussing legislative history and quoting S. Rep. No. 109–14 at 43 (2005)). The Ninth Circuit 
26  has cited the Senate Report on CAFA for its explanation that “because interstate class actions

28  any other type of lawsuit, the Committee firmly believes that such cases properly belong in

781 F.3d 1178, 1182

13                    IV.  AWARD OF FEES AND COSTS                           
14      Plaintiffs request an award of fees and costs in connection with remanding this action to 
15  King County Superior Court. “An order remanding the case may require payment of just costs 
16  and any actual expenses, including attorney fees, incurred as a result of the removal.” 28 U.S.C. 
17  § 1447(c). According to the Ninth Circuit, “[a]bsent unusual circumstances, a court may award 
18  costs and attorney’s fees under § 1447(c) only where the removing party lacked an objectively 
19  reasonable basis for seeking removal.” Grancare, LLC v. Thrower by & through Mills,
889 F.3d 20 543, 552
 (9th Cir. 2018). Where it is “obvious” that the removing party cannot prove facts 
21  sufficient to justify removal, an award of fees and costs will be upheld.
Id.
 
22      Plaintiffs contend that it is obvious both that the potential plaintiff class contains less than 
23  100 individuals and that the claims here arise out of plaintiffs’ ownership of securities. Dkt. # 7 
24  at 25. Plaintiffs’ first argument, regarding the numerosity requirement, is easily dispatched. 
25  Defendants have presented credible evidence in the form of Kenck’s declarations that 
26  demonstrates that defendants had an objective basis for believing that the numerosity 
27  requirement was met. Dkts. # 18, # 32.
